paragraphs: This checklist is for self-questioning only and does not constitute hiring criteria, ability scores, or physical fitness evaluation conclusions. This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2011.00 “Firefighters” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation, and the body text follows that official occupational scope). Even within fire service positions, the differences are large: municipal firefighting and rescue, employer-based full-time fire brigades, forest and wildland firefighting, airport and industrial firefighting, emergency medical and hazardous materials handling, and fire equipment operation and training. Before comparing positions or development paths, first check: the education and fire academy or on-the-job training required for the role, whether certificates such as emergency medical technician (EMT) are required, physical fitness test, medical, and background check standards, the duty system (commonly a 24-hour shift schedule) and rotation arrangements, and the safety and personal protective requirements for on-site work.

Validate with one paper exercise: you are given a completely fictitious firefighting and rescue assignment (building type and number of floors, seat of the fire and smoke spread conditions, locations of trapped people, available fire apparatus and water sources, order of arrival and crew assignments). You are asked to write out the initial on-arrival assessment points and what to report, hose and nozzle selection and the water supply plan, forcing and ventilation methods, the search route and safe withdrawal conditions, whom to coordinate with, and to mark which decisions must be made by the on-scene commander.

Signals worth considering more: able to accept high-intensity physical work and on-scene risk, willing to act according to orders and procedures, and able to stay calm and look after teammates in a tense scene. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to keep up long-term physical training and duty, difficulty accepting danger and uncertainty, and treating the firefighter image from film and television as the daily work.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute hiring, ability scoring, physical fitness, or safety conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to make firefighting, rescue, and on-scene handling a long-term career: it requires maintaining physical fitness over the long term, acting according to orders and procedures in dangerous environments, taking on emergency medical and hazardous materials handling tasks, and accepting a 24-hour shift system and rotations; validate with the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page.

The work of firefighters revolves around the cycle of “alarm and response—on-arrival assessment—handling action—clearing and records—training and prevention”: on receiving an alarm, quickly don protective equipment and board the apparatus; on arrival, assess the fire conditions and report to the commander, lay hose lines, connect water sources, select nozzles and extinguishing agents, and carry out firefighting as required; at the same time carry out forcing, ventilation, and search and rescue, move trapped people to a safe area, and provide emergency medical treatment such as first aid and CPR to the injured; take containment and control measures for hazardous materials that may ignite, leak, or spill; after the fire is extinguished, check the scene to eliminate reignition hazards, clear standing water and forcing damage, and protect undamaged property; then complete incident and rescue records, take part in drills, skills training, and physical training, and carry out public fire prevention outreach and inspections. The emphasis differs greatly by direction: municipal firefighting and rescue stresses arrival speed and teamwork, emergency medical work stresses on-scene assessment and handover to transport, hazardous materials handling stresses detection, isolation, and protection levels, forest and wildland firefighting stresses terrain, wind direction, and water supply conditions, and equipment and training positions stress vehicle and equipment operation and passing on techniques.

U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2011.00 “Firefighters”: control and extinguish fires and respond to emergency situations that threaten life, property, or the environment; duties may include fire prevention, emergency medical services, hazardous materials handling, search and rescue, and disaster assistance.

Work context | Firefighters alternate between standing by at the station and on-scene handling, and on-scene work is both intense and risky. O*NET work context shows that work schedules are mostly irregular (58%), with 37% regular; among weekly work hours, 31% exceed 40 hours and 69% are less than 40 hours (survey results; the cause of the shift pattern cannot be inferred from this ratio); 29% have face-to-face discussions every day and 44% once a week or more; 40% use email every day; 86% consider the work to require extremely precise or highly accurate work combined (39% extremely important, 47% very important); the consequences of error are extremely serious for 49% and very serious for 26%; 22% have strict deadlines every day and 39% once a month or more; conflict situations occur every day for 11% and once a week or more for 25%; 50% of respondents stand more than half the working time; 47% of respondents walk or run more than half the working time; 77% sit less than half the time; 33% work outdoors in all weather every day and 44% once a week or more; 27% are exposed to contaminants every day; 32% are exposed to hazardous equipment every day; 33% are in dangerous conditions every day; 27% are exposed to high or low temperatures every day; 73% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others and 18% high responsibility; the degree of automation of the work is 32% not at all automated, 26% slightly, and 31% moderately.

Main objects | Fire apparatus and pumps, hoses and nozzles, forcing and ventilation tools, ladders and ropes, breathing apparatus and protective equipment, fire water sources and hydrants, injured and trapped people, hazardous materials and incident scenes, and rescue and drill records.

Collaboration | Collaboration with on-scene commanders and fellow firefighters on the same shift, emergency medical and hospital admitting personnel, police and investigators, hazardous materials specialists, rescued people and their families, and the community public.

Tools and materials | Fire apparatus and pumps, hoses and nozzles, forcing and cutting tools, ladders and lifting equipment, self-contained breathing apparatus and personal protective equipment, thermal imaging and gas detection devices, communications and dispatch equipment, and first aid equipment and automated external defibrillators.

Institutional basis | Fire and rescue and emergency response procedures, hazardous materials management and handling regulations, occupational safety and health requirements, fire vehicle and equipment maintenance standards, emergency medical treatment protocols, and duty and attendance systems.

Record requirements | Dispatch and arrival records, fireground handling and command records, casualty treatment and transport records, equipment inspection and maintenance records, and training and drill records must be kept on file according to institutional rules.

Practice boundaries | Fireground command authority and emergency handling decisions are made by the on-scene commander according to procedures; matters involving enforcement, accident determination, hazardous materials handling, and medical treatment authority must be carried out by authorized personnel and professional bodies, and this page does not provide rescue tactics, medical, or safe-operating advice.

Environment and pace | On-scene conditions involve risks of high heat, heavy smoke, collapse, electricity, chemicals, and work at heights; response and handling times are concentrated and unpredictable, standby must be maintained while at the station, and duty often uses a 24-hour shift system including nights and holidays.

Region and scope | U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2011.00 does not map one-to-one onto mainland China's occupational classification; the mainland's fire and rescue force system, occupational qualifications, physical fitness assessments, and duty systems must be verified separately according to local regulations.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2011.00 “Firefighters” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation): control and extinguish fires and respond to emergency situations that threaten life, property, or the environment. Specifically this includes: after an alarm, donning protective equipment such as fire-resistant clothing and breathing apparatus and driving the fire apparatus to respond; on arrival, assessing the fire conditions, building structure, and dangers and reporting to the commander; laying hose lines, connecting water sources, selecting nozzles and extinguishing agents, and operating pumps to fight the fire; forcing open doors, windows, and roofs to create ventilation and entry; using ladders to reach upper floors and search for and rescue trapped people; providing emergency medical treatment such as first aid and CPR to the injured; taking containment and control measures for hazardous materials that may ignite, leak, or spill; after the fire is extinguished, checking the scene to eliminate reignition hazards, clearing standing water and forcing damage, and protecting undamaged property; completing incident and rescue records; and taking part in drills, skills and physical training, and carrying out public fire prevention outreach and hazard inspections.
entries.question: What do Firefighters mainly do?

entries.answer: Primary tasks and authority differ: this occupation's main output is firefighting, rescue, and on-scene emergency handling, and it also handles emergency medical care and hazardous materials; fire inspectors and investigators focus on premises inspection, permits, and fire cause investigation under fire codes and belong to the enforcement and investigation category; fire prevention and protection engineers produce technical solutions for fire protection systems and building fire protection design; emergency management directors focus on plan development, resource coordination, and interagency coordination; emergency medical technicians focus on prehospital emergency medical care and transport and usually do not fight fires; police and patrol officers focus on public order maintenance and criminal enforcement; and occupational health and safety specialists focus on workplace hazard identification and safety management.
entries.question: How does it differ from fire inspectors and investigators and emergency medical technicians?

entries.answer: U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2011.00 “Firefighters”: interest code R, Job Zone 1-2 (requiring little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), not marked as Bright Outlook (projected average growth of 3% to 4% for 2024—2034). Definition notes: wages, employment, and growth are on the exact occupation definition (2025 median hourly wage $28.50, median annual wage $59,280; the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles about 34,910, 44,490, 77,250, and 101,040 USD / year respectively; 2024 employment about 344,900; average annual job openings about 27,100). BLS OOH separately gives 355,300 employed in 2025, 4% growth for 2025—2035, an increase of about 13,100, and about 26,800 average annual openings, which is on a same-period definition and marked in the body text. The education survey has published the leading items (high school diploma or equivalent 70%, postsecondary certificate 12%, less than a high school diploma 11%), the remaining items are not published, and this page does not fill them in.

entries.answer: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (requiring little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0). Work context shows that work schedules are mostly irregular (58%), with 37% regular; among weekly work hours, 31% exceed 40 hours and 69% are less than 40 hours (largely affected by the 24-hour shift system); 86% consider the work to require extremely precise or highly accurate work combined; the consequences of error are extremely serious for 49% and very serious for 26%; 22% have strict deadlines every day; conflict situations occur every day for 11%; 50% stand more than half the time every day; 47% walk or run more than half the time every day; 33% work outdoors in all weather every day and 44% once a week or more; 27% are exposed to contaminants every day; 32% are exposed to hazardous equipment every day; 33% are in dangerous conditions every day; 73% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others; the degree of automation of the work is 32% not at all automated, 26% slightly, and 31% moderately. Duty often uses a 24-hour shift system including night and holiday response.
entries.question: What are the daily work context and preparation level like?

entries.answer: The more accurate judgment is that steps such as dispatch order assignment, information lookup, and record and training material organization will be taken over by tools, and the occupation as a whole will mainly see augmentation. The ILO 2023 study shows that task exposure varies greatly across occupations, that the share of highly exposed tasks in managerial and professional occupations is relatively low, and that technical feasibility does not mean agencies have already adopted it; on-scene assessment, search and rescue decisions, safety judgments, and command responsibility must be borne by trained personnel, so the conclusion is that the way of working will change, not that the occupation as a whole will be replaced.

entries.answer: For this exact occupation in 2025, the median hourly wage is $28.50 and the median annual wage is $59,280; the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles are about 34,910, 44,490, 77,250, and 101,040 USD / year respectively (May 2025 OEWS, presented via O*NET). The 2025 median annual wage given by BLS OOH is also $59,280 (hourly $28.50). The median is the midpoint of the wage distribution of the employed, not a starting wage; OEWS is on an employed-person definition and does not include volunteer firefighters, and BLS has not published a readable figure for this occupation's industry-specific wages. Personal income also depends on region, rank, duty allowance, and overtime arrangements.

BLS indicates that the typical entry-level education is a postsecondary non-degree award, usually with no related work experience required and long-term on-the-job training needed, and that most people are trained at a fire academy. In mainland China, a high school education or above, fire academy or on-the-job training, and physical fitness assessment are commonly required; the specifics are subject to the job posting and local regulations.
entries.question: What education and qualifications are required?

entries.answer: Most regions and employers require completion of fire academy training and may require certificates such as emergency medical technician (EMT), a physical fitness test and medical examination, and a background check; some positions also require fire vehicle and equipment operation qualifications or specialty training in special rescue and hazardous materials handling. These requirements vary by state or locality and must be verified against the original text of the target employer, the competent department, and local regulations; this page does not provide legal or compliance advice and does not equate a certificate with on-scene handling ability.
entries.question: What certificates or permits are required?

entries.answer: Responsibility for on-scene handling and for one's own and teammates' safety is borne by duty personnel; fireground command authority and emergency handling decisions are made by the on-scene commander according to procedures, and matters involving enforcement, accident determination, hazardous materials handling, and medical treatment authority must be carried out by authorized personnel and professional bodies. The scene must be worked according to handling procedures and personal protection requirements, with the withdrawal route and safety conditions confirmed before entering; rescue records and information about casualties and involved parties are kept confidential according to institutional rules. When using dispatch and monitoring type tools, tool outputs do not constitute command orders or accident conclusions, and matters beyond one's training and authorization are handed to authorized personnel. This page does not replace fire and rescue and emergency response procedures, hazardous materials management and handling regulations, occupational safety and health requirements, emergency medical treatment protocols, or vehicle and equipment maintenance standards.

subject.name: Firefighters
subject.summary: Control and extinguish fires and respond to emergency situations that threaten life, property, or the environment: includes driving and operating fire apparatus and equipment, wearing protective equipment such as fire-resistant clothing and breathing apparatus, connecting high-pressure hose lines and operating pumps and nozzles to extinguish fires, forcing open doors, windows, and roofs to create ventilation and entry, using ladders to reach upper floors or rescue trapped people, searching for and rescuing trapped people, providing emergency medical treatment such as first aid and CPR, handling hazardous materials that may ignite or leak, protecting property from water and smoke damage, and participating in drills, training, fire inspections, and public fire prevention education.
